target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it brings convenience, productivity, health, accessibility, and safety benefits.
objection: AI may offer conveniences, but its overall societal impact is negative because it increases economic insecurity through automation and concentration of profits, undermines critical thinking, reproduces racial bias, and creates major privacy risks that outweigh the benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is inherently bad because of jobs, critical thinking, bias, and privacy harms.
objection: Those harms do not make AI inherently bad; they can be reduced through responsible deployment, including worker reskilling, educational safeguards, fairness auditing, and privacy-preserving techniques, so AI can still be good for society when governed.

target: AG1’s assumption that guardrails such as reskilling, classroom oversight, audits, and privacy protections can keep AI’s harms under control.
objection: Governance is structurally hard to implement at AI’s speed and scale, so the promised safeguards are unlikely to keep up with real-world deployment; as a result, harms remain persistent and the benefits are not enough to make AI good overall.

target: AG2’s claim that governance cannot keep up and therefore AI is net harmful.
objection: Governance is not all-or-nothing: AI can be regulated with risk-tiered controls, liability, and existing legal frameworks such as labor, consumer-protection, anti-discrimination, and workplace-safety rules, making responsible deployment practical and enforceable.

target: AG1’s claim that risk-tiered regulation and accountability can reliably control AI harms.
objection: Even risk-tiered regulation runs into major practical limits: models are opaque, auditing is constrained, deployment is faster than oversight, enforcement varies by jurisdiction, and competitive pressure pushes vendors to ship systems before safeguards are effective.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity, deployment speed, and enforcement gaps make AI governance ineffective.
objection: Those are deployment challenges, not reasons to reject AI: high-risk uses can be restricted through procurement and licensing, monitoring can be continuous rather than one-time, AI itself can help with oversight, and low-risk uses can still deliver net social benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that procurement, licensing, monitoring, and AI-assisted oversight can reliably prevent the worst harms.
objection: Those measures still do not reliably stop harm because AI-based oversight can reproduce the same biases, many risky uses fall into gray areas that evade classification, and governance can be captured by industry or weakened by limited expertise and vendor dependence.

target: AG2’s claim that human review and due process cannot prevent harmful AI decisions.
objection: AI can be used only as decision support, with final human judgment, documented reasons, and user recourse; properly designed human-in-the-loop systems and contestability mechanisms can reduce harm without rejecting AI overall.

target: AG1’s claim that human-in-the-loop review, due process, and appeals will prevent AI harms.
objection: In practice those safeguards often fail because humans rubber-stamp AI outputs, proprietary systems cannot give actionable explanations, and accountability becomes diffused so institutions can hide behind “human approval” while harms continue.

target: AG2’s claim that human review and appeals fail even with better system design.
objection: The failure of naïve human-in-the-loop systems is not a reason to reject AI; better workflows such as uncertainty thresholds, standardized logs, and audit trails can make accountability real and keep AI beneficial.

target: AG1’s claim that better workflows, logs, and audit trails can make AI accountable and prevent harm.
objection: Even with those mechanisms, real-world power asymmetries, compliance costs, and cognitive offloading mean most people cannot effectively challenge harmful decisions, firms can treat penalties as a cost of doing business, and widespread reliance on AI erodes critical thinking and contestability.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s worst harms cannot be reliably prevented.
objection: Society can capture the benefits by using a portfolio approach: expand low- and medium-risk applications first, such as accessibility tools, tutoring, and safety monitoring, while pausing or restricting the highest-risk uses until they meet stringent conditions.

target: AG1’s portfolio strategy that keeps safer uses while restricting the most dangerous ones.
objection: Portfolio control breaks down because AI platforms spill from low-risk uses into higher-risk ones through mission creep, even helpful tools still create privacy and bias harms, and business incentives push companies to monetize the same systems in riskier ways.

target: AG2’s claim that mission creep and repurposing make the portfolio strategy unworkable.
objection: Spillover can be prevented through purpose limitation, data governance, technical and organizational isolation, and gated approval for expansion into higher-risk uses, so portfolio deployment can remain beneficial while limiting repurposing.

target: AG1’s claim that purpose limits, isolation, and gated expansion can stop spillover.
objection: Those safeguards are hard to enforce in practice because firms reinterpret purposes, infrastructure is shared across supposedly isolated systems, regulatory gates depend on vendor-controlled evidence, and privacy harms can occur through leakage or inference even without deliberate repurposing.

target: AG2’s claim that safeguards are too hard to enforce for AI to be net good.
objection: AI can also defend society by adding provenance and verification tools and by improving learning; it can strengthen critical thinking through better tutoring and help society detect misinformation and manipulation when deployed with verification safeguards.

target: AG1’s claim that provenance, watermarking, and tutoring will protect critical thinking and reduce misinformation harms.
objection: Those defensive tools are fragile: watermarking can be evaded, detection cannot scale as fast as generation, and repeated reliance on AI explanations and drafts encourages cognitive offloading rather than independent verification.

target: AG2’s argument that AI’s risks justify broad rejection.
objection: Rejecting AI ignores the opportunity cost of losing real, immediate benefits such as accessibility tools, tutoring support, health assistance, and workplace-safety improvements; society can instead steer deployment toward high-value uses and restrict the riskiest ones.

target: AG1’s claim that society can steer AI toward benefits while restricting harms.
objection: The tradeoff is artificial because many useful functions can be provided by non-generative or privacy-preserving alternatives, the same platforms still carry privacy and bias risks even in low-risk applications, and the harms of AI are systematic rather than incidental.
